text: Ferenc Bedő / Age: 33
Rank/Position: Private (enlisted soldier), infantryman
Civilian Occupation: Railway worker (switchman / track switch operator)
Origin: Szolnok County, Great Hungarian Plain
Bedő Ferenc was “Ferkó” to everyone back home.
He had to be. His father was Bedő Ferenc, too. And his father before him.
You can't spend your whole life shouting “Hey, Feri!” into a room
and expect the right man to turn around,
so you have to distinguish somehow.
That's how a strange thing happened: Ferkó grew into a giant.
104 kilos. 193 centimeters.
He stood a head and a half above his father — Older Bedő Ferenc —
and his grandfather — Even Older Bedő Ferenc. And still, as “Ferkó”,
he was the one who felt like a dumb child.
Just because he'd made the mistake of being born 22 years after one of them, and 39 years after the other.
Now he grips his rifle and fires into a horizon that looks impossible to reach.
He thinks he would give almost anything to hear someone call him Ferkó one more time.
But there's no chance of that here. When they drafted him, he introduced himself as Ferenc.
Not Feri. Not Fecó. Not Ferchi. Ferenc.
And because he used to be so big, so strong, every man in this trench has called him Ferenc ever since.
He's shrunk since then. Starved down. Folded in on himself.
But the name stayed. It clings to him like mud.
And every time someone says it, it sounds hollow. Foreign.
Like they're calling to somebody else,
and his body just happens to answer.
Last night, chewing on tough, salty beef, he felt an urge he couldn't swallow.
To tell someone.
To let the nickname exist out loud.
There was a man beside him in the trench,
maybe five years younger.
They shared a torn blanket.
If Ferenc remembered correctly, the man — János — was from the same part of Hungary.
Somewhere around Szolnok.
That was enough to make Ferenc feel a kind of kinship,
so he decided János was the right witness for a confession like that,
even though he didn't look like a soldier, not really.
Back home, he could've been a librarian. A teacher.
A watchmaker. A doer of some kind of womanly profession.
His fingers were long and spidery,
and even after weeks out here,
his nails still looked strangely kept.
So Ferenc told him. He said the thing he'd been holding in. And János didn't answer.
At first, Ferenc got angry. Then the anger curdled. Disgust. Panic.
He saw the glassy stare. He lifted the blanket, searching for the wound.
A bullet hole. Blood. Anything. There was nothing.
János had simply frozen to death.
The boots on Ferenc's feet are János's boots. Inherited.
No. Stolen. Taken to replace Ferenc's own shredded pair.
And now they squeeze his toes painfully.
The pain makes it hard to do the only job he has left:
to keep firing at the Soviets across the river.
So there's the cold. And the bullets whipping over his head.
And now this, too.
He almost wishes it would all just end.
That wish lasts only until he hears it: the dull thump of a body hitting the ground a few meters away.
The sound brutally reminds him that cold, fear,
and pain are still better than non-existence.
Between two shots, Ferenc repeats something to himself. Over and over. Like a prayer, like a plan.
If he ever gets lucky enough to introduce himself to a new person again, he'll say the following:
<i>“Bedő Ferenc. The younger one.
But you can just call me Ferkó.”
